Neil thinks 90% of AI workloads will run in the background versus real time.

In that future, latency matters less and cost matters more, and he's configured his company around a unique way of serving tokens at the cheapest possible price.

"There's no bad chips. There's only bad pricing, and I will make any chip work at the right price. Let's talk about AMD, great chips overall. 

People don't understand how to program them very well. That's music to my ears. I'm happy for them to sleep on this chip and for me to buy as much as I can."

"One of the ways I describe what we do is, we will buy any chip anywhere in the world for any duration of time. 

That is a level of flexibility and liquidity that no one else has right now. You'd have basically zero buyers for a data center that is ninety-five percent uptime. I'm that first buyer. 

First we scavenge chips, and then we scavenge power for those chips. 

The idea is, in both cases, I do not want to be bidding against Anthropic or OpenAI for compute capacity. I'm not gonna win against them, and I don't want to. 

I want to be more creative and use the supply that they don't find legible today. 

Over time I amass enough aggregate supply...and build my aggregate factory that is unbeatable in economics."

"My whole goal is to so dramatically expand the supply of power across the United States that I have a home for a lot of chips that otherwise would not have earned their place in a data center."

"We've really pushed AI to be an interactive chatbot tool, and everyone has chosen latency optimization because the shape of usage was chatbot oriented. 

That's the most profound change we're going to see in the next year, we're gonna move away from chatbots to more proactive or background agents, and in that world, it makes a lot more sense to build a stack around throughput."

"I love this market because it's unbounded. There's no human in the loop, so you can consume as many tokens as you like in the background versus human attention span. 

So long term, we're going to end this year at maybe fifty-fifty background and real time workloads, but I see this going to ninety ten in favor of background."

"The best latency is no latency at all. When you wake up in the morning, the work's already been done overnight, you didn't even have to ask for it. 

What we'd like is the agent to operate on more human time scales. You don't manage your colleagues every five minutes. You come back and check in maybe once a week."

"My job is to make the tokens as cheap as humanly possible, and I will do it through every layer in the stack available to me."

A good example comes from a 16th-century English village. A farming household might include not only parents and their children, but several unrelated teenagers or young adults. They were called “servants,” who were the children of other farming families who had temporarily left their own homes to work for wages. A farmer’s 16-year-old son or daughter, for example, might leave their parents, move several villages away, and spend a few years working in another household. They each would later marry and establish households of their own. Historians such as Peter Laslett and Richard Wall refer to this period between leaving the parental household and marriage as “life-cycle service.”
This created a distinct period between childhood and marriage. By his early 20s, a young Englishman might already have spent years earning wages, living among strangers, going on adventures, changing employers, and moving between communities and villages. Independence (in the modern sense) was, therefore, experienced well before the formation of a family of one’s own.

→ BTC: +$1.9B
→ ETH: +$700M

So did these inflows drive the rally, or were they the result of it?
A bit of both.

Flows were already positive on Aug 17–18, but they accelerated after Aug 19, when BTC and ETH had already started breaking higher. ETF buyers helped support and extend the move, but they weren’t the only reason behind the rally.

And most of the ETF demand came through @BlackRock:

→ IBIT: ~69% of BTC inflows
→ ETHA: ~77% of ETH inflows

Simply put, BlackRock is way too powerful.

Shout out to the Coinbase listing team.

For years now I’ve been sharing horror stories about CEXs that I’ve picked up from founders, other investors and industry insiders, about how shady exchanges and their listing teams enrich themselves at the expense of both founders and their own user base through listings.

Turns out it didn’t fall on deaf ears. 

The Coinbase listing team themselves reached out to me, because they saw my criticism, appreciate it, and are always open to feedback on how they can keep improving their listing processes.

Had an extensive call with them about it, and while it wasn’t particularly surprising, the Coinbase listing team is probably one of the very few that is genuinely trustable and compliant. They don’t try to squeeze founders, they simply list the best assets that people actually want, and they genuinely care about the industry for the long term.

I found it really impressive how transparent they were, walking me through everything from front to back, sharing how their listing processes work and how they try to strike the right balance between memecoin listings and fundamentally strong projects.

And even more impressive was how genuinely interested they were in my takes on what could still be improved in the listing process, what I’d like to see, and how they can ultimately become an even better exchange. They genuinely care and listen.

Really like how they’re approaching listings, for two reasons:

1) they are truly 100% free. And I mean 100% free, no hidden costs like airdrop budgets or range rovers that come attached.

2) while volume should be their main focus and KPI as a business, they try to optimize for what’s best for their user base and this industry overall.

Much smarter and more long term oriented than many of the other shady CEXs that just try to extract as much as possible in the moment.

It goes to show once again why Coinbase is the oldest and most trustable exchange out there. 

They’ve always played the honest, long term game, and it has paid off big time so far. I don’t expect it to be any different this time.

After all, here’s what makes me happiest about all of this:

Massive confirmation that it’s worth speaking up, and that we don’t always have to just accept everything and swallow it.

It might not be much, but I’m proud to be contributing to a better industry, and I’ll keep doing so.

You can do it too.

87% of the top 100 coins are back above their 50-day trend.
A month ago that number was closer to 36%.

BTC's getting close to $80K and the price targets are already flying.

Does this mean alt season's starting?

Well, the main thing I'm watching is who's doing the buying.

The move started like a classic squeeze. Short liquidation levels were stacked right above BTC, and buyers came in hard around the mid-$60Ks. Once price pushed into those levels, the forced buying did the rest.

But the squeeze isn't really what's carrying this anymore. BTC and ETH ETFs pulled in around $3B over the last 7 days, and spot buying ran about $1.5B on BTC and $805M on ETH.

So there's a real bid under this rally now.

The catch is that the biggest chunk of that bid are coming from ETFs. That's great for Bitcoin's price, but it's not the same thing as retail flooding back into crypto.

So no, alt season isn't starting. This is BTC and institutions pulling the market out of a hole.

Meanwhile, traders are getting aggressive again. Open interest is climbing, funding's already at 0.94%, and the futures premium is widening.

People went from scared to paying roughly 13% a year just to stay long, and it took about three days for that switch to happen.

That's the part that makes me nervous. When the long side gets this crowded and levered, one bad headline is all it takes to kick off a liquidation cascade.

The early bull signs are real.

But retail is nowhere in sight, and leverage is rebuilding faster than the demand underneath it. 

A few things that would make me get more aggressive:
• ETF inflows holding near that $3B weekly pace instead of fading
• Funding and the futures premium cooling off while price holds
• Breadth staying above 80% through the first real pullback
• Dominance slipping under 59%, which is the actual rotation signal

So, what am I doing? I'm accumulating majors, slowly. The whole reason these prices exist is that retail isn't back yet, so waiting for them to show up before you bid kind of defeats the point. 

By the time your group chat is asking about crypto again then BTC’s gonna be 100k.

Be smart about it. No chasing, and no leverage. The recovery looks real to me, and so does the cascade risk. 

There’s going to be flush imo. You wanna be the one who buys and benefits from it than the guy getting liquidated.
